title: How does South Carolina handle NIL era? Dawn Staley gives blunt take
text:

Dawn Staley gives blunt take
 Meghan L. Hall USA TODAY Nov. 20, 2026, 6:06 p.m. ET Hear this story Dawn Staley revealed one way the South Carolina Gamecocks tackle NIL and recruiting in women's college basketball .
 "When you're recruiting young people and their families, we like to throw the number out there before they even come to campus. Either you're going to come to campus, and we can just get down to the business and having a good time and seeing if you fit here," Staley said . "For us, we've stuck to our numbers because that's the numbers that we have. We're not inflating ... and if we get more money, we say, 'Hey, we'll share it,' but you gotta stick to it ... I gotta draw the line where I have to draw the line."
 Staley told the media Friday the NIL money players receive is good no matter where they may land. Yet, the Gamecocks coach detailed multiple things she says money cannot do.
 "Money really can't make you feel better. Money can't make you play better," Staley said. "Money can't drive you when you're not playing how you visualized, and for us, we got all those other things outside of the high price tag of paying players a lot of money with all the other stuff: the comfort stuff, knowing that this is hard. This is hard, and no matter how much money a kid makes, if they are unhappy, they are going to be unhappy, and we try to provide making them happy."
 Over the last five years, Staley, like many others across college basketball, has navigated the NIL landscape. She's been successful, winning three championships, signing sought-after transfer portal targets and some of the country's best high school players. This year alone, Staley landed four prospects in the class of 2027, including the No. 4 ranked player, Jezelle "GG" Banks .
 WOMEN'S SPORTS: The latest news and insider insights from USA TODAY Studio IX. Staley emphasized Friday that South Carolina isn't "cheap" when it comes to recruiting talent, but the Gamecocks coach says the program is honest about what it can do for players.
 "We say what we have for certain players, and if they want it, great. If they don't want it ... I'll say this: if somebody's paying twice and three times as much as us, I say go get the money. Like really. It's generational wealth for some kids. We make a lot of money. Like we make a lot of money," Staley said. "If somebody said you can only make a certain amount, and that's it, we would wrestle with that, right? And it's all (about) what people are willing to pay."
 Staley is the third high-profile coach in recent days to be asked about the challenges of overseeing a program during the NIL era. UConn coach Geno Auriemma and UCLA coach Cori Close also spoke openly about what they face.
 "We just signed the No. 9 player in the country. We don't have cachet with guys that are getting paid a million dollars to go play some place," Auriemma said. "They're getting the cachet. I just don't see the value of paying a high school kid a million dollars to come out of high school that hasn't dribbled the ball one time in college."
